html:
In September and October 1835 the young Charles Darwin spent five weeks on the Galápagos Islands, a group of volcanic islands on the equator about 900 kilometres west of Ecuador. He was the naturalist on HMS Beagle, a British navy ship surveying the coasts of South America.

He collected birds, plants, lizards and tortoises. The local vice-governor told him he could tell which island a giant tortoise came from by the shape of its shell. Darwin also noticed that the mockingbirds differed from island to island. Only after he got home did experts show him that his small brown birds, now called Darwin's finches, were many separate species with beaks suited to different foods.

These clues helped convince him that species are not fixed but change over time, each island's form adapting to its home. Over the next twenty years he worked out his theory of evolution by natural selection, published in On the Origin of Species in 1859. The islands have been a living laboratory of evolution ever since.
